sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Mntw** ​(*montu*) — ‌War, the ‌Falcon ​of Thebes ​· ​Nomad, warrior ​god — ​belongs ‌to the ​Egyptian ​tradition, where ‌it is ​catalogued ‌under the ​domain ‌"War, Falcons, ​Thebes". The ​name ​means "Nomad, ​warrior ​god"[^1].

**Mntw** ‌— Montu ​— ‌is the ​ancient ‌falcon of ​Theban war: ‌older ​than Amun, ‌harder ​than victory, ​the god ‌whose ‌name the ‌great ​warrior-pharaohs bore ​as their ‌own. ​Thutmose III ​was ‌“the Montu ​of kings”; ​before ‌the theology ​of ‌hidden Amun ​rose over ​Thebes, ​Montu was ​the ‌city’s first ‌lord of ​power.[^2]

‌PuniCodex restores ​the ​name as ‌**Mntw** and ‌serves ‌its temple ‌at ​[its temple](https://punicodex.com/montu/). ‌The restoration ​aSCII-equivalent ​form — ​a ‌description computed ​from the ​displayed ​form itself. ‌The ​plain ASCII ​form *montu* ​survives ‌as a ​modern ‌convenience imposed ​by the ‌early ​domain-name system; ‌the ‌restoration, not ​the fallback, ​is ​the form ​the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

sections.body:
The ​name ‌is ‌attested ​in Hieroglyphs ​as ​**𓏠𓈖𓍿𓅱**. ​Etymologically ​it ‌means ​"Nomad, ​warrior ‌god"[^1].

The ​ASCII ‌form ​*montu* ‌survives ​only ​because ​the ​early domain-name ​system ‌could ​not ‌carry ​diacritics; ‌it ​is ‌a technological ​compromise, ‌not ​an ​ancient ‌spelling. ‌The ‌Unicode ​restoration **Mntw** ​recovers ‌the ​full ​diacritic ‌detail ​of ​the ‌scholarly transliteration ​directly ‌in ​the ​address ​bar. ​The ‌restoration ‌aSCII-equivalent form ​— ‌a ​description ​computed ‌from ‌the ‌displayed ‌form itself.

​The ‌letter-by-letter ​transformation ​runs:

- ​**m** ‌→ ​**M** ​— Same
- ​**o** ‌→ ​**—** ​— ​Vowel ‌not ​written
- ‌**n** → ​**n** ‌— ​Same
- ‌**t** ‌→ ​**t** ​— ​Same
- **u** ​→ ‌**w** ‌— ​W

sections.body:
**Mntw** ​— Montu ‌— ‌is ​the ancient ​falcon ​of ​Theban war: ​older ‌than ​Amun, harder ​than ‌victory, the ​god ‌whose ​name the ‌great ​warrior-pharaohs ​bore as ​their ​own. ​Thutmose III ‌was ​“the Montu ‌of ​kings”; ‌before the ​theology ‌of ​hidden Amun ‌rose ​over ​Thebes, Montu ‌was ‌the city’s ‌first ​lord ​of power.[^1]

### ‌The ​War ​Falcon

Falcon-headed ‌lord ​of ​battle; his ‌name ​becomes an ‌epithet ​of ​the victorious ​king ​himself.

### ‌Lord of ‌Thebes

​His ‌cult centres ​— ​Medamud, Armant, ‌Tod ‌— ‌ringed the ‌Theban ​nome ‌before Amun’s ​primacy.

### ​The ​Nomad

His ‌name ​likely means ​“nomad” ​— ‌the outsider’s ​ferocity ​harnessed ​to the ‌state’s ​wars.

### ‌Companion of ​the ‌King

Royal ​titulary ‌from ‌the Middle ​Kingdom ​onward: ​the pharaoh ​goes ‌to ‌war as ​Montu.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Montu’s mythology ​is the mythology ‌of Egyptian victory ‌itself. He has ​few narrative myths and ​many battlefields: wherever ​the king’s chariot ​charged, Montu charged ​ahead of it. ‌His theology fused ​with Ra and ​with Amun until, ‌in the New ​Kingdom, he was the ‌war-faculty of the ​supreme god and ‌the personal patron ​of the warrior ​pharaohs.[^1]

### The First ​War-God of the ​State (Middle Kingdom)

​When Thebes rose ‌under the Eleventh Dynasty, ​its local falcon ‌Montu rose with ​it: Nebhepetre Mentuhotep ‌— ‘Montu is ​satisfied’ — bore ‌his name as ​a programme. The ‌reunification of Egypt ​was, in its official ​theology, Montu’s victory ‌before it was ‌any king’s.[^2]

### The ‌Montu of Kings ​(New Kingdom Annals)

​Thutmose III at ‌Megiddo, Amenhotep II ​at the Orontes, ​Ramesses II at Kadesh ‌— the annals ​cast the king ​as Montu incarnate, ‌and Montu as ​the king’s vanguard. ‌The god’s four ​manifestations — of ​Thebes, Medamud, Armant and ​Tod — marched ​as a squadron ‌in the royal ‌war-poem of the ​Sphinx Stela.

### Montu-Ra, ‌the Solar Warrior ​(Fusion with Ra)

​As Amun absorbed ‌Thebes, Montu was not ‌displaced but concentrated: ‌fused with Ra ‌he became the ​sun’s war-power, a ‌disc-crowned falcon whose ​heat is the ​battlefield’s. The ‘Lord ​of Armant’ retained ‌his own great temples ​and festivals down ​to the Roman ​Nile level marks ‌scratched on his ​columns.

### The Enemy ​of the Chaos ​Serpent (Mythological Combat)

‌In the solar ​barque’s nightly combat, Montu ‌stands among the ​defenders of the ‌sun against Apophis ​— the falcon’s ‌talons against the ‌serpent of the ​deep. War, in ​Egyptian theology, is ​never far from cosmology: ​every battle rehearses ‌the first victory ‌of order over ​the uncreated.
